content: Sulfa drugs, also known as sulfonamides, are a class of medications that include antibiotics such as sulfamethoxazole, sulfasalazine, and sulfacetamide. It is critical to differentiate sulfa drugs from other sulfur-containing compounds like sulfates and sulfites, as these are chemically distinct and do not provoke the same hypersensitivity reactions associated with sulfonamides. Sulfonamide antibiotics are employed in the treatment of various infections, including Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, urinary tract infections, shigellosis, and certain protozoan infections. Beyond their antimicrobial applications, the sulfonamide chemical structure is also found in non-antibiotic medications, such as thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, metolazone, indapamide), sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide, glyburide), and acetazolamide. Sulfasalazine, in particular, is used not only as an antibiotic but also in the management of inflammatory bowel disease. Adverse reactions to sulfonamide antibiotics occur in approximately 3% of the general population. However, the prevalence of hypersensitivity reactions is significantly higher in individuals with HIV, reaching approximately 60%. Patients who exhibit hypersensitivity to one sulfonamide antibiotic are likely to experience similar reactions to other drugs within the same class. In contrast, hypersensitivity reactions to non-antibiotic sulfonamides are less common. Although there is some debate, current evidence suggests that individuals with hypersensitivity to sulfonamide antibiotics do not have an increased risk of reacting to non-antibiotic sulfonamides. The hypersensitivity reactions associated with sulfonamide antibiotics are linked to two specific regions of their chemical structure. The first is the N1 heterocyclic ring, which is responsible for type I hypersensitivity reactions. The second is the N4 amino nitrogen, which undergoes a stereospecific metabolic process to form reactive metabolites. These metabolites can induce either direct cytotoxicity or an immunologic response. Non-antibiotic sulfonamides lack both of these structural features, which may explain their lower risk of hypersensitivity reactions. The most common hypersensitivity reactions to sulfa drugs include rash and hives. However, severe and potentially life-threatening reactions can also occur. These include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, agranulocytosis, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and fulminant hepatic necrosis, among others.
